For example, among men who described themselves as having traditional values, the model predicted that 16% would see men and women as similar in workplace abilities, compared with 56% in the survey. Sequential completion has mixed effects on joint validity, and reversing question order produces different joint distributions in both tested cases. Order checks and classical marginal bounds clarify what can be assessed before linked validation answers are available. The findings support validating the joint events a simulation uses and separating empirical constraints from model assumptions. The evidence concerns selected binary tasks and one model version.

title: Inference After Model Refutation: Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models
abstract: When data reject an econometric model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others, even when that inference is exact. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. With repair-by-repair primitive bounds, PR equals the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with the band, so no smaller band-based set has the same guarantee. I derive limits on learning the repair, the exact perturbation radius of the minimal-repair correspondence, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and a reduced-form version valid at zero first stages. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument should be dropped, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect of institutions.

title: Not Strassen's theorem
abstract: Suppose there is an uncertain state of the world, drawn from a CDF G. It is well known that the random posterior mean induced (via Bayes's rule) by a signal must have a distribution F that is a mean-preserving contraction of G, and conversely that any mean-preserving contraction is induced by some signal. This is not Strassen's (1965) theorem! It is a distinct result, versions of which were stated (or at least alluded to) by Hardy, Littlewood and Polya (1929), Blackwell (1951) and Kolotilin (2014). I give a precise statement and a complete proof.

title: Factors Influencing Rural Female Workforce Participation in India, 2017- 2025: An Econometric Analysis Using District-Level Panel Data
authors: Bishwanath Goldar and Suresh Chand Aggarwal
abstract: Rural female workforce participation rate (RFWPR) in India declined between 1993-94 and 2017-18. After 2017-18, the trend reversed, and RFWPR rose from 23.7% in 2017-18 to 44.9% in 2025. Using district-level panel data for about 500 districts for nine years, 2017-18 to 2025, the paper analyzes econometrically some key determinants of RFWPR in India in the recent period. We find that the presence of young children in the family tends to reduce RFWPR, consistent with findings from several previous studies. Our econometric model results indicate that an increase in household real income, proxied by the monthly per capita consumption expenditure deflated by the consumer price index, tends to reduce RFWPR. Increases in the real wage rate of casual workers in rural areas, likely reflecting a shortage of such labour, particularly in agriculture, tend to raise RFWPR. However, the positive effect of wage hikes on RFWPR continues only until real rural wages reach a particular level. Beyond that wage rate, the positive effect of wages on RFWPR diminishes or could even turn negative, i.e., rural wage hikes tending to reduce RFWPR.

title: A Modified Glicko Model for Rating Soccer Clubs and National Teams Worldwide
abstract: Comparing soccer teams that rarely or never meet is a fundamental challenge in sports analytics: clubs play mostly within their national leagues, and national teams within their confederations. We propose a rating framework that places clubs and national teams worldwide on a common probabilistic scale. Building on a recent extension of Glicko with order effects and strength-dependent draw probabilities, we adapt the model to soccer with goal-scoring adjustments, a decomposition of home advantage, extra time, league-aware rating initialization and rules of promotion and relegation that do not inflate the levels of leagues; national teams start from the levels of their confederations. The models are evaluated on about 1.2 million club matches of 252 leagues from 166 countries (2000-2026) and 12.6 thousand national team matches (1998-2026). On held-out seasons, the modified Glicko model is clearly more accurate than Elo and as accurate as score-matrix models built on the goal expectations of a gradient boosting model, including the Dixon-Coles and Markov chain models, while it is substantially more accurate in international club matches. Averaging the predictions of the rating model and the Markov chain model is more accurate than either model alone. For national teams, the model is significantly more accurate than all baselines, especially in the final tournaments, where teams of different confederations meet. The resulting ratings are interpretable and can be used for player evaluation, transfer analysis and match forecasting. The match data, the ratings and the code are publicly available at https://github.com/andreyshelopugin/SportsRatings

title: From the firm- to the application-level: A new typology of AI use in organisations
abstract: Artificial intelligence is applied in organisations in many different ways. However, the firm-level literature on AI lacks a conceptual framework able to describe that variety. Empirical studies typically examine one dimension of AI use at a time. This paper argues that the difficulty follows from the unit of analysis: a firm may hold many AI applications at once, each with its own novelty, sourcing mode, objective and technology type. These dimensions are defined at the level of the application rather than of the firm. We therefore propose shifting the unit of analysis from the firm to the individual AI application, and develop a typology combining these four conceptual dimensions. The new framework locates any application in a common space, and it points out in particular two types that the prevailing adoption-innovation distinction neglects: co-invention, novel uses of technology the firm did not develop, and internalisation, in-house building of AI that could have been bought instead. Documented use cases illustrate the framework, which is then used to discuss implications for firms strategies and the diffusion of AI in economic systems.

title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
authors: Cinzia Di Nuzzo and Matteo Farn\`e
abstract: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
abstract: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
authors: Nina Effenberger and Florian E. Roemer and Maybritt Schillinger and Maxim Samarin and Erich Fischer and Reto Knutti
abstract: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
abstract: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.

title: Super Learner: A Practical Tutorial
abstract: The selection of an optimal predictive model is a pervasive challenge in biostatistics and epidemiology. Relying on a single a priori algorithm risks overfitting and reduced generalizability when applied to new settings. Super Learner is a flexible ensemble machine-learning method that mitigates these risks by combining multiple candidate algorithms into a single prediction model. Using cross-validation, it defines a weighted combination of learners that minimizes a specified loss function, ensuring performance asymptotically equal to or better than the best candidate algorithm. This tutorial provides a comprehensive, practical guide to implementing Super Learner in R for applied researchers. Using a simulated epidemiological dataset with a binary outcome, we demonstrate the step-by-step construction of the ensemble. We cover the foundational statistical concepts, basic implementation, evaluation through cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, feature screening, and performance optimization for metrics such as the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). Additionally, we detail advanced usage, including computational parallelization and the integration of custom algorithms and screening procedures. The guide also includes a consolidated section on best practices for specifying SL, covering loss function selection, effective sample size determination, CV scheme definition, library curation, and discrete vs. ensemble SL decisions, plus a practical reference to the caret package for model preprocessing and comparison. This guide equips epidemiologists and clinical researchers with the tools to confidently incorporate robust machine learning techniques into their predictive modeling workflows.

title: Fr\'echetFlow: Flow Matching for Non-Euclidean Data
abstract: Scientific observations such as probability distributions, trees and covariance matrices call for generative models that respect their non-Euclidean geometry. While flow matching has been extended to manifolds by utilizing geodesics and velocities, such manifold structures are not available in a general metric space. We introduce Fr\'echetFlow, a generative modeling framework for metric space-valued data that requires neither linear operations nor a smooth manifold structure. A key feature of the proposed approach is that we utilize well-established Euclidean flows to learn the joint distribution of distances to a set of landmarks, whereupon new objects are reconstructed from generated landmark representations. The reconstruction step utilizes weighted Fr\'echet means of reference objects, drawing on Fr\'echet regression. We establish Wasserstein error bounds that connect accuracy of the generated object distributions to the placement of landmarks, flow approximation and reconstruction error and prove consistency under finite second moments. This leads to convergence rates that depend on the metric complexity of the target objects, tail moments and fitting accuracy. Experiments show competitive accuracy with established flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and lower Wasserstein errors than specifically tailored methods for several scientific datasets. Across simulation settings, we find that generation error decreases as sample size increases.

title: Structural Analysis of Object-Valued Time Series
abstract: We develop inference for structural patterns in the temporal association of object-valued time series. Our framework is built on pairwise lag profiles, which record the expected value of a chosen pairwise function at each lag and serve as a unified inferential target. We consider three representative structural features: whether a profile reaches stability beyond a finite lag, remains constant over time, and displays geometric regularity at short lags. To assess these properties, we design statistical tests calibrated by a common block multiplier bootstrap that accommodates serial dependence and the overlap inherent in lagged pairs. Gaussian approximation results establish bootstrap validity for asymptotic size control, while suitable signal conditions guarantee consistency against the corresponding alternatives. Finite-sample performance is examined through simulations in both Euclidean and density-valued settings. Applications to electricity load curves and stock-return distributions illustrate how the proposed procedures characterize association across lags.

title: Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching: Frozen Estimation and Adaptation
abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.

title: Improving Efficiency and Power in Small Rare-Disease Trials Through Prespecified, Data-Adaptive Covariate Adjustment
abstract: Covariate adjustment can potentially improve efficiency in randomized clinical trials, but in rare diseases, limited prior knowledge makes it difficult to specify an adjustment at the design stage. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) with the Super Learner (TMLE+SL) can outperform fixed adjustment methods, such as the G-computation estimator, by leveraging machine learning to learn both the covariates and the functional form of the adjustment from the trial data. Estimating the known treatment mechanism can improve efficiency further. In simulations reflecting real rare-disease trials, TMLE+SL yielded valid inference and achieved greater efficiency and power than conventional analyses. Finally, we also provide practical guidance on specifying TMLE+SL in rare-disease trials.

title: Common-DAG Support from Targeted Covariance Changes under Confounding
abstract: Targeted covariance changes couple structural rows through a common directed acyclic graph. We study the graph support determined by these experiments when structural errors may be correlated. A positive-gap four-node family has a shortcut identified by common acyclicity. A response indegree of at most two additionally gives unique complete support and two compatible coefficient matrices. The same experiments admit a stable feedback model with the shortcut absent. The result extends to connected graphs with repeated branching and merging. Finite response-column alternatives yield exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions through Horn propagation and partial-target completion. Certified ancestry then supplies an observed-ancestor covariance restriction. Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion reduce inference to a scalar confidence set, and quadratic elimination retains the shared nuisance coefficients with finite-sample edge-error control. In 2048 Gaussian conditions, the scalar procedure reports 127/128 positive edges at gap 1/4 and 524288 observations per cell. Its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference on the same inputs in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact 16-, 32- and 64-node evaluations verify support and target-coverage conclusions. A root-target characterization connects the identifying information to intervention design.

title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
abstract: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

title: The Cherry-Picking Trap
abstract: When a better-informed proposer puts forward a policy proposal, the responder should not take the proposal at face value but ask why it was chosen. We model how this inference can undermine trust even when interests are broadly aligned. A proposer privately observes a "basket" of viable policies and proposes one; a responder decides whether to approve the proposal but may lack the expertise to evaluate it. A larger basket makes a Pareto improvement more likely to be available but also gives the proposer greater scope to cherry-pick a policy that favors him at the responder's expense. In the unique equilibrium, Pareto improvements are often proposed and yet rationally rejected. Flexibility that should enable agreement instead breeds distrust.

title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
abstract: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
abstract: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

title: Generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty
abstract: In this paper, we study generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty, where the random intercept has mean uncertainty and takes values in an unknown bounded interval. We develop a novel two-step method, named Firth-corrected Expectation-Maximization with Moving Block (FEMMB), to estimate the regression coefficients as well as the lower and upper bounds of the intercept. A Firth bias correction is incorporated into the EM algorithm to mitigate the incidental parameters problem, which is prominent in generalized linear models with many nuisance intercepts. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimated regression coefficients, and the consistency of the estimated intercept bounds. Simulation studies and a real-data application to an imbalanced credit card dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Nested Ensemble Learning with Topological Data Analysis for Graph Classification and Regression
abstract: We propose a nested ensemble learning framework that utilizes Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to extract and integrate topological features from graph data, with the goal of improving performance on classification and regression tasks. Our approach computes persistence diagrams (PDs) using lower-star filtrations induced by three filter functions: closeness, betweenness, and degree2 centrality. To overcome the limitation of relying on a single filter, these PDs are integrated through a data-driven, three-level architecture. At Level-0, diverse base models are independently trained on the topological features extracted for each filter function. At Level-1, a meta-learner combines the predictions of these base models for each filter to form filter-specific ensembles. Finally, at Level-2, a meta-learner integrates the outputs of these filter-specific ensembles to produce the final prediction. We evaluate our method on both simulated and real-world graph datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking methods, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error. It also surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, ranking among the top three models across all benchmarks.

title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
abstract: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Fairness under Data Imbalance: Theory and Adaptive Allocation
authors: Kaifeng Zhang and Anru R. Zhang
abstract: Data imbalance across sensitive groups and class labels is common in classification problems and can contribute to substantial fairness disparities. We study how such imbalance affects Equal Opportunity and how synthetic data augmentation can mitigate the resulting unfairness. We first identify two mechanisms, prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance, through which changes in the training distribution shift the learned decision boundary and induce disparities in group true positive rates. Motivated by this analysis, we study exact full-balance augmentation, which equalizes all group-label cells. We establish conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity together with a prediction-error comparison under the oracle balanced distribution, and show that the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as the sample size grows and the generator error vanishes. The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
abstract: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer. Such equilibria suffer lost gains from trade both due to the inefficiency introduced by screening (as in independent private value settings) and due to adverse selection. We identify broad conditions under which, nevertheless, sequential equilibria are guaranteed to achieve a constant fraction of the first-best gains from trade. Our bounds quantify the central role of rare pessimistic seller signals and rare optimistic buyer signals. The results apply to seller-proposer, buyer-proposer, and random-proposer mechanisms. The key idea in our analysis is to relate equilibrium gains from trade to proposer profits in an auxiliary market with independent private values.

title: A Geometric Perspective for Marginal R2: Estimation and Inference in Generalized Linear Mixed Models
abstract: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) are widely used across scientific disciplines, yet quantifying response variation explained by auxiliary information remains challenging for non-Gaussian outcomes and hierarchical dependence. Existing $R^2$ measures provide useful summaries, but their variance-based constructions are not generally linked to a common geometric interpretation, a fixed-design marginal estimand, and corresponding statistical inference. We propose marginal quasi-$R^2$ through two distinct operations. First, marginalization integrates over latent random effects, retaining their uncertainty in the marginal response moments and specifying the model for explanatory assessment. Second, a Quasi-GLM formulation supplies a local working information metric under which orthogonal projection yields an Pythagorean decomposition of explained and unexplained variation. We define a fixed-design population estimand, establish consistency and asymptotic normality of its estimator, and derive cluster-robust sandwich standard errors and confidence intervals under stated regularity conditions. Simulations assess estimation accuracy and interval coverage across response families and random-effects structures. Two ecological applications illustrate the importance of reporting estimation uncertainty alongside marginal quasi-$R^2$. The method is implemented in the R package quasiR2.

title: Lost in the Bins: Treatment Effects with Discretized Covariates
abstract: Mean independence restrictions are widely used to identify average treatment effects, but the covariates used to formulate these restrictions are often observed or used in coarsened form. This paper shows that mean independence conditional on a finely measured covariate need not hold after the covariate is replaced by a coarsened version. Coarsening can therefore change the identifying content of the comparison rather than only the precision of estimation. I characterize the resulting coarsening bias for the ATT and ATE. For the ATT, the bias is driven by within-cell composition in untreated potential outcomes. For the ATE, an additional treatment effect heterogeneity term appears. I then introduce $c$-mean dependence, a nonparametric relaxation of exact mean independence at the coarsened level, and derive sharp bounds for average treatment effects. The parameter $c$ determines how far comparisons may extend across neighboring values of the coarsened covariate. I propose sample analogue estimators and bootstrap inference procedures for the resulting bound functions. In an application to voluntary military service using data from Angrist (1998), positive effects on early earnings, which primarily reflect military pay, hold even under the weakest form of $c$-mean dependence, whereas the evidence on later effects on civilian earnings is inconclusive once mean independence is relaxed.

title: Semiparametric Inference for Marginal Win Odds with Censored Time-to-Event Outcomes
abstract: Win statistics provide clinically interpretable measures for comparing treatment groups with prioritized composite outcomes, but efficient covariate-adjustment methods for win statistics with right censored time-to-event outcomes remain limited. We develop a semiparametric framework for marginal win probability and win odds with prioritized time-to-event outcomes, including semi-competing risks, while also accommodating scalar survival outcomes as a special case. The estimand compares independent draws from the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes under treatment and control, which preserves a marginal causal interpretation. We derive the efficient influence function under conditional independent censoring, allowing censoring to depend on baseline covariates and predictable event history. The resulting cross-fitted one-step estimator incorporates covariate adjustment and censoring martingale augmentation, allows flexible estimation of nuisance parameters, and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound under suitable conditions on consistency and convergence rate of nuisance parameters. Simulation studies show that the estimator has small bias, accurate standard error estimation and confidence interval coverage, and substantial efficiency gain relative to the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted (IPCW) estimator. An application to a randomized breast cancer trial comparing tamoxifen combined with radiotherapy against tamoxifen alone demonstrates improved precision, with an approximately 25\% reduction in estimated variance at five years.

title: Identification of Rational Inattention-Additive Random Utility Models
abstract: This paper introduces a novel class of econometric models, called Rational Inattention-Additive Random Utility Models. It is based on the discrete choice rational inattention model of Matvejka and McKay (2015) with additive unobserved heterogeneity incorporated. We show that some of the systematic components of the primitives of the model are nonparametrically identified even if the distributions of unobserved variables and the prior of decision makers are both unknown to the Econometrician. If additional information about the prior is known to the Econometrician, even stronger identification results become available.

title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
abstract: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. In these settings, classic distribution comparison tools such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) can be systematically biased, matching artifacts of the measurement process rather than the underlying mechanisms of interest. We study a practical regime in which noisy observations are abundant, but only a small audited subset contains ground-truth measurements. We propose measurement-error-corrected MMD (MEC-MMD), an audit-based estimator that debiases kernel evaluations without requiring a noise model. MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing, admits an explicit variance decomposition, and is consistent for the population MMD, achieving the standard $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ rate when the audit size scales with the dataset. We demonstrate the utility of distributional matching with MEC-MMD loss for both parameter estimation and unsupervised applications, showing that MEC-MMD consistently outperforms MMD and alternative methods. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

title: Asymptotic Consistency of a Weighted Nadaraya-Watson Estimator Driven by Fractional Brownian Motion at Random Times
abstract: Nonparametric regression conventionally assumes equispaced observations, a premise often violated by empirical data with irregular sampling and long-memory noise. This study establishes the asymptotic mean square ($L^2$) consistency of a weighted Nadaraya-Watson (wN-W) estimator for stochastic processes sampled at random times and perturbed by fractional Brownian motion (fBm). Leveraging the occupation time formula and Fernique's Theorem, we derive exact parametric restrictions on bandwidth and sampling rates ensuring convergence. We validate these theoretical findings via extensive simulations evaluating the mean squared error under varying noise persistence. Crucially, we explicitly benchmark the performance of the estimator under random sampling times against classical deterministic grids, while assessing the relative efficiency of quartic versus Gaussian kernels. Finally, we introduce an interactive Shiny application to dynamically visualize the admissible parameter space, and we empirically validate our theoretical framework by applying the estimator to the Vostok ice core paleoclimatological dataset. This real-world application demonstrates the practical capacity of the methodology to extract macroscopic trends while robustly avoiding severe overfitting under random sampling times.\

title: Martingale posteriors for flexible regression via recursive least squares
abstract: Predictive Bayes quantifies uncertainty by specifying a sequence of one-step-ahead predictive distributions, inducing a martingale posterior without an explicit prior. Existing parametric constructions rely on stochastic-gradient updates and have seen limited development for flexible regression. We propose a predictive Bayes framework based on recursive least squares, whose martingale posterior has an explicit representation: given future covariates, it is the law of the posterior mean plus a weighted series of independent draws from the standardized predictive distribution. The posterior mean is a penalized least squares estimator, available in closed form and invariant to data ordering, whereas the predictive distribution, for example heavy tailed, is chosen separately without changing the estimator or algorithm. We derive the exact posterior variance under a known design and an asymptotically Gaussian approximation, and obtain the martingale posterior in closed form for Gaussian predictive distributions. Posterior draws are independent by construction, with a known truncation error, and require no Markov chain Monte Carlo. The construction extends to additive, mixed and Gaussian process models. In simulations and an analysis of NHANES triglyceride data, the method attains accuracy comparable to that of a fully Bayesian model with the same response distribution at a fraction of its computational cost.

title: Methodological Pitfalls in Predicting Ship Turnaround Time at Brazilian Ports: An Empirical Audit and a Reproducible Pipeline
abstract: Two recent studies on ship turnaround time at Brazilian ports report models with R-squared scores above 0.80 on data from the national waterway transportation agency. We audit their published datasets and reveal these results are inflated by structural data leakage. Specifically, 97 percent of berthing events in their random row-level split appear in both training and testing partitions. We demonstrate that a model's R-squared drops from 0.82 to 0.20 when the data is properly split at the berthing level. We further document additional methodological flaws, including survivorship bias, undocumented target truncation, and the retention of variables that algebraically reconstruct the target. To address these issues, we propose a reproducible pipeline that aggregates cargo to the berthing level, utilizes conditional imputation, and represents high-cardinality cargo variables through weighted averages of multilingual sentence embeddings. Evaluating six time targets and thirty seeds, our pipeline reveals that cargo embeddings yield statistically significant improvements on four operational targets, while administrative waiting times remain unaffected. Prior works missed this per-target heterogeneity by conflating genuine signal with leaked identity.

title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age
abstract: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects. We find that activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, while those less prevalent tend to gain share. Within AI-related work, demand is becoming more diverse, and job postings combine tasks that were rarely requested together before the generative AI era. AI-related postings also have substantially larger project budgets and involve more hours of work, while differences in hourly rates are small. Together, these findings suggest that AI is reshaping not only which tasks clients outsource, but also how they combine tasks into larger, higher-value projects.

title: Recent developments in spatial econometrics
abstract: We conduct a non-exhaustive survey of the recent spatial econometrics literature by placing it in historical context and mapping current trends. The focus will be primarily on methodological aspects. Starting from the canonical spatial autoregressive model, we cover its many extensions and richer parameterizations. We discuss spatial panel data models and advancements in the study of nonlinear and nonparametric models. Specification testing for spatial econometric models, with its roots in the $J$-test of Davidson and MacKinnon (1981), is also covered, as is spatial correlation robust inference. Finally, we review advancements in general limit theory, limited dependent variable models, spatial weight matrix estimation and endogeneity, recent attempts at uniting the network formation and spatial literature, and sundry important topics. We take stock of the current paradigm and critically evaluate the impact of the spatial literature on applied practice.

title: Orthogonal Sparse Subgraph Alignment for Structure-Function Coupling in Brain Networks
abstract: Characterizing the relationship between brain anatomical wiring and functional coordination remains a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. This difficulty primarily arises because structure-function coupling in the human brain is spatially heterogeneous, often localized to subnetworks, and inherently difficult to align across disparate representational modalities. We introduce Orthogonal Sparse Subgraph Alignment (OSSA), a principled and interpretable framework designed to identify compact structural cliques that exhibit maximal concordance with functional connectivity (FC) across subjects. Within each FC-derived community, OSSA optimizes an alignment objective over an orthogonal transformation, which absorbs coordinate mismatch between the two connectivity modalities, and a sparse node-selection vector, which identifies the induced structural connectivity (SC) subgraph. Furthermore, for canonical OSSA within a fixed population community, we establish local statistical guarantees under the required assumptions. With high probability, an empirical local maximizer exists in a specified neighborhood of the population target, and every local maximizer in that neighborhood exactly recovers the active support and satisfies a nonasymptotic error bound for the aligned functional projector. Extensive empirical evaluations on simulated data, alongside analyses of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) baseline and longitudinal cohorts, demonstrate that OSSA successfully recovers aligned structural cliques under latent cross-modal rotations. Ultimately, the proposed methodology significantly improves out-of-sample SC-FC alignment over size-matched baselines and identifies compact structural supports with longitudinal consistency in node selection, while multi-support diagnostics suggest a dominant aligned core within the estimated FC communities.

title: Hypothesis testing for estimable parameters with missing data: available cases or complete cases?
abstract: Whether to base inferences on available-case (AC) or complete-case (CC) estimators is a long-standing practical dilemma when data are missing. This issue has been investigated for point estimation in specific problems, but hypothesis testing has received comparatively little attention. The tools needed to address this problem are developed in a fully nonparametric framework for hypotheses concerning parameters that can be estimated through functions of vectors of $U$-statistics, under a MCAR missingness mechanism. The joint asymptotic normality of the AC estimators is established, permitting availability probabilities to vary with the sample size. The limiting covariance matrix factorizes into the complete-data covariance matrix and a matrix determined solely by the availability pattern, with both components admitting consistent estimators. This fact enables the construction of a Wald-type test statistic. The CC approach arises as a special case. These results allow AC and CC based tests to be compared, although the comparison is problem specific, which limits its practical value. Rather than selecting one approach, a test based on the maximum of the two statistics is also considered, whose critical value can consistently approximated by two bootstrap procedures. In simulations, its power lies between those of the AC and CC approaches.

title: The exact region of the Average Rectangular Volume and Spearman's rho, with an application to arachnitude
abstract: The average rectangular volume ($\ARV$) of a bivariate aggregation function is the average of its volumes over all axis-parallel rectangles of the unit square; for a copula, it is the expected copula volume of the rectangle spanned by two independent uniform points. We determine the exact region of the pairs $(\ARV(C),\rho(C))$, where $C$ ranges over all bivariate copulas and $\rho$ is Spearman's rho. The region is compact, convex and symmetric, and its upper boundary consists of three analytically parametrized arcs. A previously proposed family of shuffles of Min generates one arc, but only on part of its range; the other two arcs are generated by singular copulas whose supports contain hyperbolic branches. The boundary is continuously differentiable away from its left endpoint $\ARV=\frac{11}{120}$, where it has a vertical tangent. The proof uses a folding transformation and explicit Kantorovich potentials for a family of optimal transport problems. Finally, we show that the arachnitude, a rank correlation used in actuarial practice, is an affine transformation of $\ARV$, so that the result also describes the joint region of Spearman's rho and arachnitude.

title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.

title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.

title: One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
abstract: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUC$_\pi$, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting $\pi$ treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index $J(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) - \mathrm{FPR}(t)$ across cutoffs $t$, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid S]$; for AUC$_\pi$, the decision maker's probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUC$_\pi$ is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by $|\pi(s) - \pi(s')|$ is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUC$_\pi$, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUC$_\pi$ does not.

title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to na\"ive KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

title: Convergence and global optimality of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for Gaussian mixtures
abstract: We study explicit Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for fitting Gaussian location mixtures by nonparametric maximum likelihood. The full sequence converges weakly and has finite length in the bounded-Lipschitz metric throughout the original step-size range. These conclusions hold for any fixed data set in any dimension and any initial probability measure. By an earlier conditional optimality theorem, the limit maximizes the likelihood under full-support initialization. Fix any particle step size in $(0,1]$. Initialize the particles by resampling the observations. For an open set of triples of points in the plane, the probability of convergence to a strictly suboptimal fixed point tends to one exponentially as the particle count grows. Without reweighting, a centered Gaussian initialization can give a strictly suboptimal limit. Every finite iterate has a smooth, strictly positive density. The limit assigns positive mass to a nonglobal local maximum of the associated Gaussian sum. We also give the exact pure-transport limit for a one-dimensional initialization with full support and an atom. An exact finite-dimensional representation preserves the truncated likelihood moments and the retained region's contribution to the current dissipation. This lets us transfer an analytic gradient inequality to the measure trajectory.

title: Cotangent-lift inference of stochastic microbial dynamics
authors: Jos\'e A. Capit\'an and Alberto Meg\'ias and Cristina Sard\'on
abstract: We study the parameter estimation for the stochastic logistic and Lotka--Volterra diffusions from discrete, irregularly spaced observations corrupted by measurement noise, a setting typical of microbiome time series. For the logistic equation, the growth rate acts as a time change and does not enter the stationary law, so it can be identified only from the temporal structure of the data. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimator of the Euler scheme, with the observations taken as the states, coincides with the regression of log-increments on abundances used in the literature, and we characterise what this estimator cannot see under measurement noise: for the linearised dynamics, the law of consecutive pairs of observations is invariant along an explicit one-parameter family of relaxation rates and noise levels, and the regression converges to a limit set by the noise. Treating the true abundances as latent, we compute the likelihood with a Gaussian moment filter and show that measurement noise is precisely what couples the filter states across samples. The exact gradient is then the backward recursion of the discrete cotangent lift, whose cost, two to three likelihood evaluations, does not depend on the number of parameters, and we give the covector map of each filter step in closed form. In simulations, the latent estimator recovers the relaxation times, noise levels and interaction strengths that the regression biases, while larger communities require prior information on the interactions. In gut microbiome time series it attributes most of the variability of a dominant genus to measurement noise and estimates its relaxation time at about $64$ hours, with a large standard error.

title: Semiparametric Inference in Panel Data with Interactive and High-dimensional Confounding
abstract: This paper develops inference for a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in partially linear panel models with high-dimensional observed covariates and latent interactive confounding. Flexible adjustment for observed covariates can leave correlated factor components in treatment and outcome residuals, invalidating standard double/debiased machine learning (DML). We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML), which estimates treatment-side and reduced-form factor spaces from first-stage residuals. The estimator combines a feasible double projection with three-fold, unit-level cross-fitting. The double projection controls interactions between the two estimated factor spaces. The separate folds eliminate same-training-unit pairings in the leading disturbance components of the factor-estimation errors. Under fixed factor ranks, pervasive factor signals, strict exogeneity, and joint asymptotics in the number of units N and periods T , FA-DML is first-order equivalent to an infeasible oracle, is asymptotically normal, and admits consistent variance estimation. In the baseline simulation design with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML confidence intervals have coverage close to the nominal level. Standard DML and a two-fold variant that estimates both factor spaces on the same units substantially undercover. In an application to U.S. states, FA-DML finds that a 10% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across control sets and first-stage learners.

title: A Bayesian approach for checking and estimating block designs in agricultural experiments
abstract: Spatial blocking is a common technique used in designed agricultural experiments. Spatial blocking, however, requires important assumptions about the spatial dependence patterns in the field. Statistical models of blocked agricultural experiments often show spatial structure in the residuals, suggesting that the original model may benefit from additional assumptions regarding the spatial dependence patterns present in the field. We propose a Bayesian model for checking block membership and estimating spatial patterns missing in the original block design. Our model is particularly motivated by cases with mis-specified blocks. To accomplish this, we embed a regression tree within a Bayesian statistical model to estimate spatial effects with a block-like spatial structure. We illustrate the benefits of our model using simulated data mimicking four typical scenarios we have encountered in our applied experience in agricultural research and using two datasets generated from designed agricultural experiments. We found that our model may serve two purposes: validating the originally designed block layout, or mis-specified block-like spatial structures. Thus, our model provides researchers with a novel tool for analyzing data from designed agricultural experiments.

title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.

title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

title: Probabilistic Upscaling of the Interfacial Transition Zone Behaviour in Concrete
abstract: The stiffness and cracking behaviour of concrete are influenced by the interfacial transition zone (ITZ), the thin shell of paste that surrounds each aggregate. Yet the ITZ's mechanical properties are poorly characterized and are usually assigned to mesoscale models through ad hoc reduction factors. Because the ITZ is only tens of micrometres thick, its stiffness must be inferred indirectly from micromechanical tests, and the resulting estimates vary widely between studies and are rarely reported with a quantified uncertainty. We present a workflow that calibrates a homogenized ITZ model against the surface displacements of several micro-cantilever bending specimens and returns its stiffness descriptors as posterior distributions rather than single values. The calibration is posed as a Bayesian inverse problem with a model-discrepancy term, sampled with a surrogate-assisted Bouncy Particle sampler, the first application of this sampler to a real-world engineering problem. We compare a pooled model, which fits one descriptor vector to all specimens, with a hierarchical model that treats the specimens as draws from a common population and is sampled with a local extension of the sampler. The hierarchical model separates the estimation uncertainty from the aggregate-to-aggregate material variability, where only the former shrinks as more data are added. Propagated through a representative volume element of several aggregates, its predictive yields broader distributions of the mesoscale stress and strain and a wider spread variety of maximum von Mises stress locations. The calibration places the ITZ thickness above the 30 {\mu}m to 80 {\mu}m commonly assumed in the literature.

title: Estimating multidimensional poverty under incomplete data in North Macedonia
authors: Maja Gerovska Mitev and Viktor Stojkoski
abstract: Multidimensional Poverty Indices (MPIs) are available for more than 100 countries, but rarely below the national or regional level. Local estimates require knowing how deprivations overlap within households, yet the sources that cover every locality, such as censuses and geospatial data, cannot be linked at the household level. We show how to measure local multidimensional poverty under such incomplete data, using North Macedonia as a case study. Combining settlement-level access to services with municipal census data, we pair an independence-based point estimate with sharp bounds over all joint distributions consistent with the data. We find that, nationally, 5.01 percent of households are multidimensionally poor, with bounds of 2.01 to 17.44 percent. Also, poverty is concentrated in small rural municipalities, which are poorer than nearly all municipalities of the capital city under any dependence structure. Validating our index against official statistics, the Global MPI, and a fieldwork deprivation index indicates that the socio-economic part of the index is consistent with external measures of deprivation, while the geographic part captures a distinct dimension of remoteness. Our approach thus presents a promising way to measure multidimensional poverty at the local level in countries where linked household data are unavailable.

title: How much can a human being lift? A Bayesian latent capability model for Olympic weightlifting
abstract: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.

title: Testing isotropy of random fields with values in abstract spaces
abstract: We study the problem of testing isotropy, i.e., distributional invariance under orthogonal transformations, for random fields taking values in abstract spaces. We propose a novel approach based on computing local directional characteristics, which are uniformly distributed under the assumption of isotropy. Our work is motivated by an application in material science, where we are testing the isotropy of function-valued porosity profiles of paper sheets, whose morphology is resolved by $\mu$-CT imaging. While considerably more general, the presented methodology is competitive with existing isotropy tests for real-valued random fields.

title: DynamAuction: A Reinforcement Learning Environment for Repeated Auctions with Dynamic Value
abstract: A buyer who repeatedly participates in auctions for related items often faces a dynamic value problem: what they win today changes what tomorrow's items are worth. Despite the empirical importance of such effects, especially in display advertising, the algorithmic literature on repeated auctions has largely focused on the learning problem, by treating each opportunity as a contextual bandit, while sidestepping the planning problem induced by the dependence of current value on past wins. We introduce DynamAuction, a synthetic environment for single-buyer sequential bidding. The reward from each win depends on the buyer's history of previous wins, summarized through a carry-over state. The environment supports first- and second-price auctions, non-homogeneous Poisson arrivals, delayed feedback, saturation, and recency effects. We also introduce a new class of Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithms. On our benchmark scenario, these MPC policies outperform off-the-shelf deep RL baselines (PPO, SAC, TD3) as well as a tuned shading baseline. We release DynamAuction to support RL research on repeated auctions.

title: Two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems for high-dimensional data: noncentral normal-reference inference
abstract: We study noncentral normal-reference inference for high-dimensional two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems. Within the Gaussian reference, a shifted null law is accurate if and only if covariance-weighted signal energy is negligible relative to the trace of the squared covariance. We establish the sharp uniform fourth-root error order over unrestricted spectra and a linear bound under spectral spread. A separate spectral-range criterion determines when signal magnitude alone suffices. An augmented spherical reference gives finite-sample calibration for Gaussian samples and asymptotically recovers Gaussian-reference local power under projection fourth-moment bounds and control of diagonal fluctuations, without a dimension-to-sample-size restriction. For unknown Gaussian covariance, explicit trace and hollow-Gram confidence bounds turn the linear approximation bound into a simultaneous, computable certificate over local effect ranges. Eigenspace signal energies describe directional power, while a two-point argument limits estimation of unknown local power. Simulations with 10,000 evaluation replications per configuration examine unequal and noncommuting covariances, severe sample imbalance, non-Gaussian observations and the informativeness of the certificate.

title: Deceleration without identification: testing a power-law trend in Bitcoin prices under persistent noise
abstract: Plotted against time since its first block on logarithmic axes, the price of Bitcoin lies close to a straight line, and a power law in time has been proposed as its long-run trend. A good fit is weak evidence: when deviations from a trend are as persistent as a random walk, regressions on time find trends and high $R^2$ where none exist. We first bound what fifteen years of weekly prices can reveal, then test only what is answerable. Using a few low-frequency averages, invariant to the noise scale and calibrated over a declared family of persistent deviations with a four-year cycle and declining volatility, we test constant drift in expected log price against an added log-age term. The procedure was fixed, validated and publicly hashed before it was applied once. Constant drift is rejected under this family at nominal 5%, and a log-age coefficient of 5.7, close to the published exponent, is not rejected. The rejection does not survive allowing persistence beyond a random walk, and a Gompertz curve with a ceiling fits about as well as the power law. Whether deviations revert to the trend cannot be decided. Registered forecasts for 2027-2030 will be scored by future prices.

title: Backtesting High-Dimensional Expected Shortfall
abstract: Forecast evaluation increasingly uses high-dimensional predictors, but estimation and regularization of large predictive models can distort conventional backtests. This issue is particularly important for forecasting downside risk, where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We develop out-of-sample Expected Shortfall (ES) backtests that remove the large first-order bias effects of estimating high-dimensional Value-at-Risk, ES, and the evaluation instrument. In a linear ES specification, the proposed methods are easily implemented as Double Lasso with a tail-size-adjusted score as a generated dependent variable. More generally, we characterize orthogonal ES backtesting moments, and establish oracle equivalence and valid inference under time-series dependence and repeated estimation with overlapping and expanding training windows. Simulations show that conventional backtests can severely overreject ES optimal forecasts, whereas orthogonalization improves size control. An application to downside-growth forecasting for G7 economies finds evidence against a US growth-only ES specification, even though forecast-oriented regularization selects no additional financial predictors. The application also shows that accounting for estimation can change rejection decisions in either direction. These findings highlight the distinct roles of predictive variable selection and backtesting in the evaluation of high-dimensional tail-risk models.

title: Economic Benefits of Cross-Border Electricity Trade and Domestic Electricity Production in Switzerland
abstract: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Switzerland provides a particularly compelling case because of its geographical location and limited integration into the EU electricity market. We first use the Nexus-e framework to simulate the generation capacity and transmission grid expansion required under autarky and free-trade scenarios. Based on these capacity configurations, a fundamental power market model simulates wholesale market outcomes under projected demand and generation conditions for 2040. By jointly accounting for consumer and producer surplus, as well as investments in generation capacity and grid infrastructure, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the welfare effects of cross-border electricity trade, leading to an estimated EUR 1.5 billion gain.
